say.text: Welcome to your very first class! I'll assume you know nothing yet, and that's perfect. Nothing is graded today. Just listen, and say each word back to me. Tap Next whenever you're ready, and tap any word to hear it again.
Portuguese uses the same alphabet as English, with Portuguese names for the letters. Tap any letter to hear it.
Portuguese has open and closed vowels. É with this accent is open, like e in bed. Ê is closed, like ay in they. The accent tells you which one.
The wavy line over a vowel, called a tilde, makes it nasal: the air goes through your nose. Ão sounds like owng. Listen to pão, bread.
Lh sounds like the l l i in million. Nh sounds like the n y in canyon. And an r at the start of a word sounds like an English h in Brazil: rato, mouse, sounds like hah-to.
Accents also show the stressed syllable. Café is stressed on the last syllable because of the accent.
Now your first greeting: oi, hi. Listen, and say it back to me.

rules.title: O and a: every noun is masculine or feminine

body.text: Every Portuguese noun is masculine or feminine, and “the” changes to match: o for masculine, a for feminine.
Words ending in -o are usually masculine and words ending in -a usually feminine. “My” matches too: meu gato, minha casa.

why.text: Portuguese comes from Latin, which sorted every noun into groups. The article (o, a, um, uma) shows which group a noun belongs to.

body.text: The verb's ending already says who it is, so Brazilians often drop eu (I) when it's clear: “Tenho uma irmã” is as natural as “Eu tenho uma irmã”.
É on its own means “he is”, “she is” or “it is”: “É meu irmão.”

why.text: The verb's ending already shows who is doing it, so saying eu too is often extra. Brazilians do use pronouns more than Spanish speakers, though.

rules.title: Adjectives go after the noun and match it

body.text: Most describing words come after the noun: a casa pequena, “the small house”.
They change to match: pequeno for a masculine noun, pequena for a feminine one, and add -s for more than one.

why.text: In Portuguese the noun comes first and the description follows. The ending matches so it's clear which noun it describes.

body.text: To say you're hungry or sleepy, Brazilians use estar com (to be with): estou com fome, estou com sono.

why.text: Portuguese says you are 'with' hunger or thirst: the feeling is something you have with you for now, so it takes estar com.

body.text: Put the verb straight after quero, with no extra word for “to”: quero brincar, “I want to play”.

body.text: Use estar for where something is right now: “O livro está na mesa.”

body.text: For directions, Brazilians use the polite command form: vire (turn), siga (go on), pegue (take).

why.text: Commands use a short, direct form of the verb. In Brazil, people often use the present-tense form to sound friendlier.

body.text: In Brazil, você is the everyday “you”, for friends and strangers alike. It uses the same verb form as ele and ela: “você tem”.
To be extra polite, especially with older people, say o senhor (to a man) or a senhora (to a woman).

why.text: Você is the everyday 'you' in Brazil; o senhor and a senhora show respect to older people or in formal settings.

body.text: When ordering, “eu queria” (I would like, literally “I wanted”) sounds polite. “Quero” is fine but more direct.
“Para mim…” (for me…) is the easy way to order: “Para mim, o frango.”

why.text: Eu queria uses a past form of querer to soften a request, like English 'I wanted to ask…'. Distance makes it polite.

rules.title: Me visto: verbs you do to yourself

body.text: Some verbs come with me, te or se when you do them to yourself: eu me visto (I get dressed), ele se levanta (he gets up).
In Brazil the me goes before the verb in speech: “Eu me chamo Ana.”

why.text: With these verbs you do the action to yourself, so me, te or se shows you're both the one acting and the one it happens to.

body.text: For things that happened and finished, use the simple past: fui (I went), fiz (I did), almocei (I had lunch).
Regular verbs: -ar verbs end in -ei (almocei), -er verbs in -i (comi), -ir verbs in -i (dormi).

why.text: The pretérito perfeito presents a finished action: it happened and it's done. That's why it's the tense for events.

rules.title: Two past tenses: the scene and the event

body.text: The imperfect sets the scene or says what used to happen: ela morava (she lived), andava (she would walk).
The simple past tells what happened once: ela encontrou (she found). Stories mix the two.

why.text: One past tense (the imperfeito) paints the background, the other (the perfeito) moves the story forward.

body.text: To say something had already happened before another past moment, use tinha with the participle: tinha saído (had left).
Enquanto (while) with the imperfect sets the background: “Enquanto eu cozinhava, o telefone tocou.”

why.text: Tinha plus a participle puts one past event before another, like English 'had done'.

Or point and say “Dói aqui” (it hurts here). Desde means “since”: “febre desde ontem”.

why.text: Portuguese says what hurts with doer, like Spanish: the thing that hurts is the subject, so dói matches it.

rules.title: Giving advice: deveria, se eu fosse você, and the subjunctive

body.text: “Você deveria…” (you should…) is gentle advice. “Se eu fosse você…” (if I were you…) uses a special past form.
After “recomendo que” or “é importante que”, the next verb changes to the subjunctive: durma, beba.

why.text: Advice is about what hasn't happened yet, so Portuguese uses the conditional (deveria) or the subjunctive.

rules.title: Telling a story: the linking phrases

body.text: Acontece que, 'it turns out that', brings in the twist. Resumo da ópera, 'the summary of the opera', means 'long story short'.
E pra completar, 'and to top it off', adds the last straw. No fim das contas, 'in the end', wraps up.

why.text: These phrases tell the listener where the story is going, so it feels natural and easy to follow.

body.text: Family is central in Brazil, and Sunday lunch is a big event. Bring a small gift (uma lembrancinha), like dessert.
Call your partner's parents “seu” (Mr.) or “dona” (Mrs.) with their first name: dona Maria, seu João.

why.text: Family matters a lot in Brazil, so a warm and polite first meeting goes a long way.

lines.text: Seja bem-vinda! O Pedro fala tanto de você.
lines.en: Welcome! Pedro talks about you so much.

lines.text: Muito obrigada, dona Lúcia. Trouxe um pudim para a sobremesa.
lines.en: Thank you so much, Mrs. Lúcia. I brought a flan for dessert.

lines.text: Que gentileza! Fica à vontade. Você gosta de feijoada?
lines.en: How kind! Make yourself at home. Do you like feijoada?

lines.text: Adoro! E o cheiro está maravilhoso.
lines.en: I love it! And it smells wonderful.

lines.text: É receita da minha mãe. Coma bastante, viu?

lines.text: Pode deixar. Está uma delícia, a senhora cozinha muito bem.
lines.en: Don't worry, I will. It's delicious, you're a great cook.

lines.text: Ah, que bom que gostou! Agora você já é de casa.
lines.en: Oh, I'm so glad you like it! Now you're one of the family.

body.text: Ask clearly and accept a no gracefully. “Respeito a sua resposta” says you're a good sport.
“Sem problema, foi um prazer” lets everyone leave with a smile.

why.text: Being clear and kind keeps relationships good in a culture that values warmth.

intro.text: These lines come up in the role-play “From opener to plan”. Hear them now, so you know them before it's your turn.

lines.text: Oi! Preciso saber: aquela foto na Chapada Diamantina foi antes ou depois de subir o morro?
lines.en: Hi! I need to know: was that Chapada Diamantina photo before or after the climb?

lines.text: Haha, depois! Por isso a cara de cansaço.
lines.en: Haha, after! That's why I look so tired.

lines.text: Cansada, mas com a melhor vista do Brasil. Valeu a pena?

lines.text: Cada gota de suor. E você, curte viajar?

lines.text: Muito. Estou planejando ir para o Jalapão no ano que vem.

lines.text: Sonho em conhecer! Me conta mais num café?
lines.en: I dream of going there! Tell me more over coffee?

lines.text: Fechado. Quinta, depois do trabalho, está bom para você?
